::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: BAYESIAN PREDICTIVE ENSEMBLES FOR RANDOM EFFECTS

text.text: Selecting random-effects specifications in multilevel models is challenging when several plausible alternatives exist.

Bayesian model averaging (BMA), Bayesian stacking (BS), and Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS) combine candidate predictions using weights constrained to sum to one, limiting their ability to accommodate systematic patterns beyond the candidate set.
We apply Varying Coefficient Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (VCBART; Deshpande, Bai, Balocchi, Starling, & Weiss, 2026) with an adaptive intercept to address candidate-model inadequacy.
text.formatted: We apply Varying Coefficient Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (VCBART; Deshpande, Bai, Balocchi, Starling, & Weiss, 2026) with an adaptive intercept to address candidate-model inadequacy.

text.text: VCBART estimates covariate-dependent ensemble weights without a sum-to-one constraint, allowing predictions to vary across student and school characteristics.

We compare VCBART with conventional model averaging, model selection, and alternative prediction methods through simulations calibrated to PISA 2018 U.S. mathematics data and an empirical application.

Under realistic outcome variability and moderate-to-high between-school heterogeneity, VCBART achieves the lowest out-of-sample RMSE among non-oracle methods, although its narrower prediction intervals exhibit modest undercoverage.
In the PISA application, VCBART also achieves the highest predictive accuracy, while its identified adaptive intercept reveals systematic patterns not captured by the candidate models.

In educational research, the relationship between student socioeconomic status (SES) and mathematics achievement often varies across schools, as may the effects of teacher interest, learning adaptivity, or immigration background (Goldstein, 2011; Karakus, Courtney, & Aydin, 2023; Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002).
text.formatted: In educational research, the relationship between student socioeconomic status (SES) and mathematics achievement often varies across schools, as may the effects of teacher interest, learning adaptivity, or immigration background <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Goldstein, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Karakus, Courtney, & Aydin, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these varying relationships corresponds to a different random effects specification, and choosing among them is a recurring problem in multilevel modeling.
With P predictors eligible for random slopes, there are 2 P possible random effects structures, since each predictor can either carry a random slope or not.

Prior work suggests that theory alone may be insufficient for selecting among plausible combinations of random effects, especially when fitting all candidate specifications simultaneously is computationally costly (Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily, 2013).
text.formatted: Prior work suggests that theory alone may be insufficient for selecting among plausible combinations of random effects, especially when fitting all candidate specifications simultaneously is computationally costly <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Current standard practice selects one "best" specification and proceeds as though it were the true model, discarding information in the alternatives and understating the uncertainty in subsequent inferences (Barr et al., 2013; Draper, 1995; Hoeting, Madigan, Raftery, & Volinsky, 1999; Huang & Anderson, 2021).
text.formatted: Current standard practice selects one "best" specification and proceeds as though it were the true model, discarding information in the alternatives and understating the uncertainty in subsequent inferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Barr et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Draper, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hoeting, Madigan, Raftery, & Volinsky, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Huang & Anderson, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: How much this matters depends on the inferential target.

When the goal is inference about fixed effects, valid standard errors can often be obtained from a fixed-effects or population-average model with cluster-robust standard errors, and the random-effects structure need not be specified at all (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002).
text.formatted: When the goal is inference about fixed effects, valid standard errors can often be obtained from a fixed-effects or population-average model with cluster-robust standard errors, and the random-effects structure need not be specified at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The situation is different when the goal is to predict the outcome of an individual student together with its uncertainty.
The random-effects structure then determines how a school's information is pooled with the population and which student characteristics modify that pooling.
A misspecified structure changes both point and interval predictions for that student.
This paper is about the second goal.
Individual-level prediction is a routine task in educational practice.
Early-warning systems flag students whose predicted achievement falls below a proficiency threshold so that support can be targeted (Bowers, Sprott, & Taff, 2013).
text.formatted: Early-warning systems flag students whose predicted achievement falls below a proficiency threshold so that support can be targeted <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bowers, Sprott, & Taff, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Placement and tiered intervention decisions rely on expected scores given a student's background and school.
School accountability indicators compare observed with predicted achievement at the student level before aggregating to schools (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002).
text.formatted: School accountability indicators compare observed with predicted achievement at the student level before aggregating to schools <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: In each case the prediction is made for a known student in a known school, and both the point prediction and its interval matter.

Current practice usually fits one multilevel specification, chosen by subject-matter theories or by statistical model comparisons, and treats its predictions as if that model specification were correct.
The substantive implications extend beyond statistical inference.
Different random-effects specifications can lead to different conclusions about between-school heterogeneity.

For instance, a model with a random SES slope describes how much the SES-achievement relationship varies across schools, whereas a model with a random teacher-interest slope captures a different dimension of instructional variability.
Each specification is theoretically motivated but provides only a partial representation of school-level processes.

At the individual level, a student's predicted outcome and its associated uncertainty depend on which specification is selected, and misspecification can affect both the prediction and the inference for that student.

Combining information across competing specifications while accounting for model-selection uncertainty is therefore more appropriate than selecting one and setting the others aside, particularly when predictions need to adapt to each student's own characteristics.

Bayesian model averaging (BMA; Raftery, Madigan, & Hoeting, 1997), Bayesian stacking (BS; Yao, Vehtari, Simpson, & Gelman, 2018), and Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS; Yao, Pirš, Vehtari, & Gelman, 2022) address model uncertainty through weighted combinations of candidate model predictions.
text.formatted: Bayesian model averaging (BMA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Raftery, Madigan, & Hoeting, 1997)</ref>, Bayesian stacking (BS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Yao, Vehtari, Simpson, & Gelman, 2018)</ref>, and Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Yao, Pirš, Vehtari, & Gelman, 2022)</ref> address model uncertainty through weighted combinations of candidate model predictions.

text.text: A nonparametric extension using the bracket the residual variation observed in that data, anchoring the evaluation in conditions representative of large-scale educational assessments.

Under this formulation, the weight assigned to each candidate model is estimated nonparametrically from student-and school-level characteristics, and the posterior distributions of these weights describe which specification contributes most to prediction for a given student and with what uncertainty.

The adaptive intercept absorbs outcome variance not captured by any candidate, removing the sum-to-one constraint imposed by BMA, BS, and BHS and allowing the ensemble to correct for the collective shortfall of partially specified candidates.

Among the methods compared, VCBART comes closest to the oracle in out-of-sample accuracy when within-school noise is comparable to real assessment data and between-school heterogeneity is moderate or high.
Its prediction intervals are the narrowest, at a coverage slightly below the nominal level.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
The Background section reviews the ensemble methods and the varying coefficient model that motivates the proposed approach.
The Method section describes the ensemble formulation.
The simulation and empirical studies present the evidence, and the Discussion section closes with implications for practice.

The M-Closed, M-Complete, and M-Open Settings Bernardo and Smith (2000) described three settings that characterize the relationship between a candidate model set M = {M 1 , . . . , M K } and the true data-generating process M 0 .
text.formatted: The M-Closed, M-Complete, and M-Open Settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bernardo and Smith (2000)</ref> described three settings that characterize the relationship between a candidate model set M = {M 1 , . . . , M K } and the true data-generating process M 0 .

text.text: In the M-closed setting, M 0 ∈ M, meaning one candidate is the true model, the case for which BMA was designed.
In the M-complete setting, M 0 / ∈ M but the true predictive distribution can be approximated by combining the candidates.
In the M-open setting, M 0 / ∈ M and the exact form of the true process is unknown to the analyst (Yao et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In the M-open setting, M 0 / ∈ M and the exact form of the true process is unknown to the analyst <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Yao et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The random effects specification problem examined here falls in the M-open setting.
For instance, when the true model requires five simultaneous random slopes and each candidate includes only one, the true data-generating process lies outside the candidate set.

Each partial specification still carries some information about the between-cluster structure, but constrained ensemble methods have limited capacity to correct for structural components not fully represented by any candidate model.
The adaptive intercept in VCBART is intended to address this gap.

BMA (Raftery et al., 1997) forms the posterior predictive distribution as a weighted average over the candidates, where ∆ is any quantity of interest (in this paper, the predicted outcome ŷij for student i in school j), y is the observed data, and the weights p(M k | y) are posterior model probabilities derived from marginal likelihoods.

text.text: By treating model uncertainty probabilistically, BMA propagates that uncertainty into prediction interval widths, which is the reason why it achieves near-nominal coverage in the M-closed setting (Madigan & Raftery, 1994).

text.text: When no candidate is correct, however, marginal likelihoods lose their probabilistic interpretation, and prior sensitivity becomes a concern (Clyde & George, 2004).
text.formatted: When no candidate is correct, however, marginal likelihoods lose their probabilistic interpretation, and prior sensitivity becomes a concern <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Clyde & George, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Because BMA's coherence depends on the M-closed assumption, an alternative approach is to treat model combination as an optimization problem rather than a probabilistic one.

BS (Yao et al., 2018) selects weights on the unit simplex , where w = (w 1 , . . . , w K ) ⊤ is the weight vector, by maximizing the leave-one-out log predictive density summed over the n j students in each of the J clusters, ŵstack = argmax is the predictive density of student i in cluster j under model k when that student is left out of the fit.

text.text: The objective rewards the combination that predicts best on average over students, and the predictive distribution it defines is the same mixture of the candidates as in BMA, with different weights.
The limitation is that ŵstack is a single vector for all observations, so it cannot express individual-or cluster-level variation in which candidate is relevant.
BHS (Yao et al., 2022) addresses this limitation by replacing fixed weights with covariate-dependent functions.
text.formatted: BHS <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Yao et al., 2022)</ref> addresses this limitation by replacing fixed weights with covariate-dependent functions.

text.text: For each model k and observation (i, j), the weights are obtained through a softmax transformation, where is the log-odds for model k, α 0k is the model-specific intercept, and α ℓk scales the contribution of basis function f ℓ (x ij ).
Hierarchical priors on α = {α ℓk } pool information across models.
The softmax enforces positivity and the sum-to-one constraint, and the linear predictor inside it restricts which weight surfaces BHS can represent.

For example, BHS may not detect that a random slope specification becomes relevant only above a threshold of school SES composition, or that two predictors jointly determine which specification fits best.
Both constraints carry over as limitations when the candidate set is collectively incomplete.
Related work has used BART directly to estimate input-dependent mixing weights for computer simulators (Yannotty, Santner, Furnstahl, & Pratola, 2024).
text.formatted: Related work has used BART directly to estimate input-dependent mixing weights for computer simulators <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Yannotty, Santner, Furnstahl, & Pratola, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The varying coefficient model, reviewed next, provides the theoretical basis for individual-specific weights in the ensemble setting and a nonparametric estimator that overcomes these restrictions.

The varying coefficient model (Hastie & Tibshirani, 1993) generalizes the conventional linear regression model by allowing coefficients to be functions of moderating variables: where β k (z i ) is the coefficient for predictor k as a function of the moderating variable z i , x ki is the value of predictor k for observation i, and ε i is a zero-mean error term.

text.text: Each β k varies with z i rather than being fixed across observations.
This model applies in settings where predictor effects differ across subpopulations (Fan & Zhang, 2008).
text.formatted: This model applies in settings where predictor effects differ across subpopulations <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Fan & Zhang, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In the model ensemble context, the weight w k (x ij ) plays this role.
It is the coefficient on model k's prediction in the ensemble regression, and it varies with individual-and cluster-level characteristics.
What BHS attempts through its linear parametric weights is a restricted version of this idea.
The restriction to linear forms and the softmax constraint arise from the parametric specification, not from the inferential goal.

Benchmark estimators for varying coefficient models, such as local polynomial regression (Fan & Zhang, 2008) and smoothing splines (Hastie & Tibshirani, 1993), require specifying a single scalar moderating variable and a smoothing bandwidth, making them difficult to apply when multiple student and school characteristics jointly determine model relevance.

text.text: This extension makes VCBART applicable to the random effects specification problem, where moderating variables are individual-and cluster-level covariates and the weight functions need to adapt to their joint effects without requiring the analyst to prespecify which combinations matter.
BART has also been used to estimate heterogeneous learning trajectories in large-scale assessment data (Huang, 2024), further supporting its suitability here.

text.text: As discussed in the Background section, the ensemble weight w k (x ij ) can be viewed as a varying coefficient.
It is the coefficient on the prediction from model k in the ensemble regression, and it varies with individual-level and cluster-level characteristics.
We use VCBART (Deshpande et al., 2026) to estimate these weights, following the ensemble approach introduced by Huang and Lyu (2025).

text.text: The problem formulation here differs from prior ensemble work.
The candidate models share the same fixed effects and differ only in which predictors carry random slopes.

As a result, the weight functions indicate which random-effects specifications are relevant for which students, while the adaptive intercept helps correct the shared prediction error that remains across the candidate models.
The main difference from existing ensemble methods is the adaptive intercept, which avoids imposing a sum-to-one constraint.

We write the ensemble prediction for where ŷijk is the point prediction from candidate model k, w k (x ij ) is the weight assigned to model k for covariate profile x ij , and w 0 (x ij ) is the adaptive intercept.
The weights w 1 (x ij ), . . . , w K (x ij ) are not required to sum to one.
The intercept w 0 (x ij ) plays two roles.
When the candidate models collectively underrepresent the true random effects structure, their predictions carry a systematic bias.
The intercept reduces that bias by shifting ensemble predictions away from the span of candidate outputs.
When w 0 (x ij ) ≈ 0 and k w k (x ij ) ≈ 1, the ensemble closely resembles BHS, signaling that the candidate set is adequate for individuals in that region of covariate space.
The raw intercept is not by itself the best diagnostic, however, because in this setting the candidates predict similar values.
Suppose every candidate predicts a score of 480 for a given student and let S = k w k (x ij ) denote the weight sum.

The ensemble prediction is then w 0 + 480 S. If the ensemble predicts 495, every pair with w0 = 495 -480 S fits the data equally well: w0 = 15 with S = 1, w0 = 255 with S = 0.5, or w0 = 435 with S = 0.125.
The data cannot tell these pairs apart, so the posterior of w 0 settles on whichever the prior happens to favour, and a large w 0 does not by itself mean that the candidates are inadequate.
What the data do determine is the 15 points by which the ensemble departs from the candidates.
The quantity recovers this departure, where m(x ij ) is a reference prediction that lies among the candidate predictions.
In the example, a = (495 -480 S) + (S -1) ×480 = 15 for every pair, so a is invariant to the split between w 0 and the weights.
The second term in (2) removes from w 0 the part that only compensates for a weight sum different from one.
We call a(x ij ) the identified adaptive intercept.

Any combination of the candidates whose weights sum to one can serve as the reference, such as a single candidate, BS, or BHS; the weights need not be nonnegative, but a combination whose weights sum to c ̸ = 1 predicts c times the candidates' common value, which no candidate predicts, and would shift a by (S -1)(c -1) m.
Changing the reference from one admissible m to another m ′ changes a by (S -1)(m -m ′ ), which is small when the candidates agree.
We use the BMA prediction because it is the constant-weight baseline against which the ensemble is compared throughout.
The true data-generating model is not a valid reference, since its prediction lies outside the candidate span and a would then mix the candidates' shortfall with the ensemble's own error.
When the candidates predict nearly the same value, a(x ij ) is simply the ensemble prediction minus the candidates' prediction, in score points.
Values near zero across covariate space mean that the candidates are adequate there.
Consistently positive values indicate that the ensemble predicts higher outcomes than the candidates for students with that profile, whereas consistently negative values indicate the opposite.
Either pattern marks a region where no candidate adequately captures the data and the candidate model set may need to be reconsidered.

The posterior weight w k (x ij ) describes how much model specification k contributes to the prediction for an individual with profile x ij , and the posterior uncertainty around that weight reflects how confidently that assessment can be made.
Heterogeneity therefore enters the ensemble through two different objects.

The school random effects enter only through the candidates: each candidate carries between-school heterogeneity in the form of its random slopes, and the candidates differ in which predictor is allowed to vary across schools.

The weights enter through the weight functions, which depend on the student's own characteristics, the characteristics of the student's school, and the school identifier, which is included among the inputs to the weight functions.
Within a school, the weights can differ between students whose own characteristics differ, so two students in the same school can be predicted by different mixtures of specifications.
Across schools, the weights can differ through school characteristics and identity even for students whose own characteristics are alike.
A convex combination with constant weights cannot represent either kind of variation, and BHS represents them only through the parametric form chosen for the weights.
The identified intercept adds a third layer by capturing how the candidate set as a whole falls short for each profile.
With the ensemble structure defined, it remains to specify how each weight function is estimated.
Each of the K + 1 weight components is modeled as a separate BART.

Following Deshpande et al. (2026), the weight for component k under covariate profile x is where k = 0 indexes the intercept, k = 1, . . . , K index the candidate models, T kh is the hth tree for weight function k, and µ kh is the vector of its leaf parameters.

text.text: The input x includes all individual-and cluster-level covariates, and the tree ensemble learns from data how variables and their interactions moderate model relevance without requiring prespecified functional forms.

In educational settings, VCBART can detect that a random slope for SES matters more in high-poverty schools, or that immigration-related heterogeneity concentrates in particular school contexts, without any prespecification.
Following Chipman et al. (2010), each tree is kept shallow through a splitting probability of 0.95(1 + d) -2 at depth d, which prevents any single tree from dominating the ensemble.
text.formatted: Following <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Chipman et al. (2010)</ref>, each tree is kept shallow through a splitting probability of 0.95(1 + d) -2 at depth d, which prevents any single tree from dominating the ensemble.

text.text: Terminal node parameters µ kh receive independent N (0, σ 2 µ /H) priors, where σ 2 µ controls the overall scale of the weight functions and dividing by H stabilizes their total variance as the number of trees grows.
We use H = 200 trees per weight function throughout, the default recommended by Chipman et al. (2010).
text.formatted: We use H = 200 trees per weight function throughout, the default recommended by <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Chipman et al. (2010)</ref>.

text.text: The error variance σ 2 receives an inverse-gamma prior with shape parameter ν/2 and scale parameter νλ/2, where ν = 5 and λ is set so that the prior places 95% of its mass below the residual standard deviation of a linear model of the outcome on the candidate predictions and the covariates, fitted to the training data.
Together these choices regularize the ensemble against overfitting while keeping the weight functions flexible enough to capture heterogeneous patterns of model relevance.

All K + 1 weight functions are estimated jointly through Bayesian backfitting (Hastie, Tibshirani, & Friedman, 2009), a Gibbs-like procedure in which each component is updated in turn while all others are held fixed.

text.text: Joint estimation is essential because the intercept and the model weights both depend on the outcome y ij , and estimating them separately would confound the mean correction captured by w 0 with the relative contributions of the candidate models.
The partial residuals R ijk used to update w k disentangle these effects, where 1(•) denotes the indicator function.
For the intercept update (k = 0), all candidate model contributions are removed so that w 0 captures only what the candidates miss collectively.
For model weight updates (k ≥ 1), both the intercept and all other model contributions are removed, isolating each specification's marginal contribution from the outcome.

Within each MCMC iteration, tree structures are updated via Metropolis-Hastings, leaf parameters via Gibbs sampling, and σ 2 from its conjugate inverse-gamma posterior after all weight functions are updated.
We run V = 2,000 iterations with a burn-in of V burn = 1,000 iterations, and retain all post-burn-in samples for inference.
The posterior mean weight for model k under profile with credible intervals constructed from the empirical distribution of the retained draws .
These posterior distributions are the primary inferential output.
They describe, for each individual and cluster profile, which random effects specification contributes most to prediction and with what degree of uncertainty.

Predictions for new observations are obtained by evaluating Equation (1) at the posterior mean weight functions, and prediction intervals are obtained from the posterior predictive draws, that is, the draws of the ensemble mean plus Gaussian noise with the corresponding draw of σ.

Two criteria are used to evaluate the methods.
Predictive accuracy is measured by the root mean square error (RMSE) for both in-sample (training) and out-of-sample (held-out test) observations, where N = j n j is the total number of observations.

Uncertainty calibration is measured by the empirical coverage of 95% prediction intervals, defined as the proportion of observations whose true values fall within [L ij , U ij ], the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the posterior predictive distribution.
For every method the interval is a posterior predictive interval, so that intervals are comparable across methods.
A method whose intervals miss the 95% target may not support valid inference regardless of its point prediction accuracy.
Differences between VCBART and M7 are tested with a paired-samples t test and a Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the ten shared folds.
For the PISA data, the t interval and p value are computed from the fold means and standard deviations.
Computational cost is reported in minutes of wall-clock time per fold.
All fits ran as separate jobs in a Docker container on the high-throughput computing pool, with four CPU cores for each method.
Tables 2 and 3 present in-sample and out-of-sample RMSEs.

When σ = 0.1, the outcome is nearly a deterministic function of the predictors and every candidate predicts it almost exactly, so BMA, BS, BHS, Selected, and M7 are indistinguishable both in-sample and out-of-sample.

VCBART has no shortfall to correct in this regime and pays for its flexibility with an out-of-sample RMSE almost four times that of the candidates, although still a small fraction of the outcome standard deviation of 33.

Its in-sample RMSE is close to the candidates', so the loss is out of sample: the weight functions fit the training  students and do not transfer, which is the usual cost of a nonparametric fit when there is nothing left to learn.
SoloBART is far behind at both ends (0.50 in-sample, 0.73 out-of-sample), because a sum of trees approximates a nearly linear function poorly.
The picture changes once the error is no longer negligible.

For in-sample prediction, VCBART has the lowest RMSE among non-oracle methods in every condition with σ ≥ 10 and is below M7 in eight of those nine conditions, which shows that the adaptive intercept and the covariate-dependent weights recover much of the between-school structure the candidates miss individually.

For out-of-sample prediction, VCBART is the non-oracle method closest to M7 in every condition with ICC 0.30 and σ ≥ 10 and in the ICC 0.20 conditions with σ ≥ 50, and its margin over BMA widens as between-school heterogeneity grows, from 2% at σ = 10 to about 4% at σ = 50 or 100 with ICC 0.30.
At ICC 0.10 with σ ≥ 10 the candidates differ little from one another, and BMA, BS, and Selected are ahead of VCBART by 1-2%.

The paired tests in Table 4 confirm that M7 remains better than VCBART out of sample in every simulation condition, by 2-4% at σ ≥ 10, so the ensemble narrows but does not close the gap relative to the correctly specified model.

Every method except VCBART achieves near-nominal out-of-sample coverage (94-95%) in every condition.

For BMA, BS, and BHS this holds because their predictive distributions are mixtures of the candidates' posterior predictive distributions, and each candidate is itself well calibrated for this outcome.

The mixture must be sampled as such: averaging the candidates' posterior draws with the same weights gives the same point prediction but shrinks the predictive variance whenever the weights are spread over several candidates, and the resulting intervals undercover.
With mixture sampling the three model-averaging methods are indistinguishable in calibration.

VCBART overcovers at σ = 0.1, where its intervals are far wider than the tiny residual noise, and undercovers mildly at σ ≥ 10, with out-of-sample coverage of 91-93% that declines slowly as the ICC rises.

Its in-sample coverage is within 1.5 points of nominal in those conditions, so the shortfall out of sample reflects an ensemble mean fitted closely to the training students rather than a residual variance that is too small.

The intervals VCBART produces are also the narrowest, by 4-9% at ICC 0.10 and by 15-18% at ICC 0.30, which is relevant when a decision depends on the interval and not only on the point prediction, a point we return to in the empirical study.

text.text: To target support to students at risk of falling below this baseline, a school system needs each student's predicted score and probability of falling below the cutoff, based on their background and the school they attend.
The prediction is made for a known student in a known school, so the school's estimated effect is part of the forecast.
Which random-effects specification is used changes how the school effect is pooled with the population, which student characteristics modify that pooling, and therefore which students are flagged.
We use this scenario to compare the methods on the PISA data.
The quantities of interest are the predicted score, its 95% prediction interval, and the posterior probability that the student scores below Level 2, all evaluated on held-out students.
We apply all eight methods to the U.S. mathematics data from PISA 2018 (OECD, 2019).

PISA is a triennial international assessment of 15-year-old students coordinated by the OECD and provides one of the few large-scale datasets with sufficient within-school sample sizes to support multilevel analyses with random slopes.
The U.S. sample contains 4,838 students in 164 schools.
Variable selection using lasso, random forest, and XGBoost consistently identified the same nine important predictors.

These are individual socioeconomic status (ESCS), school-level socioeconomic composition (SCHOOLESCS), school bullying climate (SCHOOLBULLYING), school immigration composition (SCHOOLIMMIG), teacher interest (TEACHINT), learning adaptivity (ADAPTIVITY), experience of being bullied (BEINGBULLIED), staff shortage (STAFFSHORT), and immigration status (IMMIG).

These span individual, family, classroom, and institutional influences on mathematics achievement (Karakus et al., 2023), and overlap with predictors examined in prior Bayesian ensemble analyses of PISA data (Huang & Kaplan, 2025; Huang & Lyu, 2025).

The six candidate models have identical fixed effects (all nine predictors) but differ in random effects structure, mirroring the simulation design.

The six candidates are close in leave-one-out predictive density on these data, with mean ELPD-LOO ranging from -3,750 (M5) to -3,747 (M2 and M3), and their out-of-sample RMSEs lie between 77.1 (M2) and 77.3 (M4 and M5).
The specification with the highest ELPD-LOO, which the Selected method uses, changes across folds: M2 in five folds, M4 in three, and M1 and M3 in one each.
No single random-slope specification is clearly preferred by the data, which is the situation in which averaging over specifications is meant to help.

This variation confirms that each predictor generates a qualitatively different pattern of between-school heterogeneity, so each candidate carries different information that the ensemble can use to go beyond what any single specification provides.

Turning to uncertainty quantification, all methods except VCBART achieve near-nominal out-of-sample coverage (94.6-95.4%), with interval widths ranging from 294 to 307 points.
VCBART produces the narrowest intervals (283 points), approximately 6.3% narrower than M7, but its out-of-sample coverage is lower at 93.3%.
Its in-sample coverage of 96.3% is comparable to the other methods.
Thus, VCBART's improved predictive accuracy and narrower intervals come with a modest reduction in out-of-sample coverage.
This pattern is consistent with the simulation findings at σ = 50 and 100, where the candidate set is collectively incomplete and the adaptive intercept provides additional flexibility.

Finally, computation times vary considerably across methods.
FE and soloBART are the fastest, requiring less than one minute, followed by M7 at 7.3 minutes.
BMA, BS, and Selected each require 27.5 minutes, including candidate fitting.
VCBART requires 35.0 minutes, approximately 7.5 minutes longer, while BHS is the most computationally intensive at 38.1 minutes.
The simulation results illustrate how the relative performance of the methods depends on the completeness of the candidate model set.
When the outcome noise is negligible, the candidates approximate the data-generating process closely, corresponding to a practically M-closed setting.
In this regime, BMA, BS, BHS, and model selection perform comparably to the oracle, while VCBART introduces unnecessary flexibility and estimation variability.
As within-school noise and between-school heterogeneity increase, the candidate set becomes increasingly inadequate, approaching an M-open setting.

Under these conditions, VCBART generally achieves the best out-of-sample predictive accuracy among the non-oracle methods, with improvements that become more pronounced as the ICC and residual variability increase.
Its adaptive intercept allows the ensemble to capture systematic patterns not represented by the candidates.
However, these improvements come with somewhat narrower prediction intervals and lower coverage.
In contrast, BMA, BS, and BHS maintain near-nominal coverage when their predictive distributions are constructed as mixtures of candidate predictions.

These findings suggest that VCBART is most beneficial when the available specifications are collectively incomplete, whereas conventional model averaging and selection remain competitive when the candidate models adequately represent the outcome structure.
The empirical analysis of PISA 2018 mathematics achievement supports these findings.
VCBART achieves the lowest in-sample and out-of-sample RMSE, outperforming both the candidate-based methods and soloBART.
It also produces the narrowest prediction intervals, although its out-of-sample coverage is slightly below the nominal level.
In contrast, BMA, BS, BHS, and model selection exhibit similar predictive performance and near-nominal coverage.
This similarity reflects the substantial overlap among the candidate specifications, which share the same fixed effects and random intercept and differ primarily in their random slopes.
When the candidates generate similar predictions, selecting or averaging among them offers limited improvements.

VCBART provides additional flexibility by capturing systematic variation beyond the candidate specifications, including nonlinear relationships with socioeconomic status and differences across student and school characteristics.
An important contribution of VCBART is its ability to accommodate individual-level heterogeneity through covariate-dependent weights and an adaptive intercept.
Unlike conventional model averaging, which assigns a common set of weights to all observations, VCBART allows the contributions of candidate models to vary across student profiles.

In the empirical application, immigration status is strongly associated with the estimated weight functions, indicating that the ensemble combines the candidate specifications differently across student groups.

Meanwhile, the identified adaptive intercept reveals systematic discrepancies between the candidate predictions and observed outcome patterns, particularly along student and school socioeconomic dimensions.
These findings illustrate how VCBART can capture subgroup-specific patterns and nonlinear relationships that are not explicitly represented in the candidate models.

However, because individual weights are not separately identified when candidate predictions are similar, they should be interpreted jointly with the identified adaptive intercept rather than as independent measures of model importance.
Together, the simulation and empirical findings highlight a trade-off between predictive flexibility and uncertainty calibration.
VCBART offers improved predictive accuracy when the candidate set is incomplete, but its narrower prediction intervals may result in modest undercoverage.
Conventional model averaging and selection provide more stable uncertainty quantification when the candidates perform similarly.
Importantly, these differences can affect substantive decisions.
In the PISA application, VCBART and the multilevel-based methods disagree on approximately 8% of student classifications relative to the proficiency threshold.
Thus, even modest improvements in predictive accuracy can lead to meaningful differences in individual-level decisions.
The proposed framework is particularly relevant to educational and psychological research, where heterogeneous relationships are common and the appropriate model specification is often uncertain.
In school effectiveness research, for example, the association between student characteristics and achievement may vary across schools (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002; Willms, 2010).
text.formatted: In school effectiveness research, for example, the association between student characteristics and achievement may vary across schools <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Willms, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Conventional approaches typically select a particular random-effects structure or average predictions using fixed model weights.

VCBART instead allows the relative contributions of candidate specifications to vary with student and school characteristics, while the adaptive intercept accounts for systematic patterns not captured by the candidates.
This flexibility is useful when researchers cannot confidently identify a single specification that adequately represents the underlying heterogeneity.
The empirical application illustrates this potential through socioeconomic status and immigration background.
The estimated weight functions vary substantially by immigration status, while the adaptive intercept captures nonlinear socioeconomic patterns and differences associated with school composition.
These findings suggest that the relevance of candidate specifications and the inadequacy of their combined predictions may arise along different dimensions of the covariate space.
Importantly, the weights are not constrained to be positive or sum to one, and their individual magnitudes may not be identifiable when candidate predictions are highly correlated.

Consequently, interpretation should focus on the overall ensemble predictions, the identified adaptive intercept, and systematic patterns in the weight functions rather than treating individual weights as model probabilities.
The broader methodological contribution extends beyond educational assessment.
Similar challenges arise in precision medicine, psychology, and other fields where heterogeneous populations are represented by competing models or latent subgroups.

Hard model selection or subgroup assignment may overlook uncertainty about which specification is appropriate for a particular individual, while conventional model averaging assumes that the relative contributions of candidate models remain constant across observations.
VCBART provides a flexible alternative by combining covariate-dependent weighting with an adaptive correction for shared model inadequacy.

This approach builds on the varying coefficient framework (Hastie & Tibshirani, 1993) and offers opportunities for extending Bayesian nonparametric methods to more complex educational and psychological measurement settings (Huang & Ghosh, 2025).
text.formatted: This approach builds on the varying coefficient framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Hastie & Tibshirani, 1993)</ref> and offers opportunities for extending Bayesian nonparametric methods to more complex educational and psychological measurement settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Huang & Ghosh, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Several limitations warrant further investigation.
First, VCBART may introduce unnecessary estimation variability when the candidate models already provide an adequate approximation to the data-generating process.
In such settings, conventional model averaging or selection can achieve better predictive accuracy and calibration with lower computational cost.

More adaptive regularization, such as shrinkage priors on the weight functions and adaptive intercept, could help VCBART reduce its complexity when the data provide little evidence of candidate-model inadequacy.
Second, improvements in predictive accuracy are accompanied by some loss of uncertainty calibration.
Both the simulations and empirical application show that VCBART tends to produce narrower prediction intervals with below-nominal out-of-sample coverage.
Stronger regularization of the tree ensemble or alternative procedures for calibrating predictive uncertainty may help address this trade-off.
In addition, the weight functions and the raw adaptive intercept are not separately identified when candidate predictions are highly correlated.

Although the identified adaptive intercept provides an interpretable summary of the correction, alternative parameterizations that explicitly separate baseline predictions from candidate-specific deviations may improve identifiability and interpretation.
Third, the simulation design considers a limited range of within-school and between-school variability under Gaussian errors and a two-level hierarchical structure.

Future research should examine more complex data-generating processes, including nonlinear covariate effects, cross-level interactions, non-Gaussian random effects, and higher levels of between-school heterogeneity.
Extensions to binary, ordinal, and count outcomes would also broaden the applicability of VCBART to educational and psychological research.
Finally, the empirical application has limitations related to the PISA data and the prediction setting.

The raw intercept w 0 and the weight sum are not separately identified when the candidates agree, and the table and the top panel of the figure show this directly.
At σ = 0.1 the weights sum to 0.12-0.16 and w 0 is 410-430, close to the outcome mean of about 480.

The top panel shows w 0 rising with ESCS from about 330 to 440 at this σ, not because the candidates fall short for high-ESCS students but because w 0 is carrying most of the candidates' own prediction, which rises with ESCS.
At σ = 10 the weight sum is close to one and w 0 sits near zero across the ESCS range.
At σ = 50 and 100 the weight sum exceeds one (1.35 and 1.48 at ICC 0.10) and w 0 moves to -170 and -230 to compensate.
The level of w 0 therefore reflects the weight sum, not candidate adequacy, and the same ensemble would show a different level under a different split.
The middle panel shows the distribution of the identified intercept after that split is removed.
At σ = 0.1 and 10 it is a spike at zero, with standard deviations of 0.4 and 2, and at σ = 50 and 100 it spreads to roughly ±40 points.

The LOESS smooth stays near zero at every σ, so the shortfall of the candidates is not a function of ESCS, and what grows with σ is the spread of individual values around thatsmooth.

The diagnostic therefore behaves as intended once the identified quantity, rather than the raw intercept, is examined: it is zero when the candidates are adequate, grows as they become less so, and does so student by student rather than along a single covariate.The weights and the identified intercept vary both across students within schools and between schools, which separates the two kinds of heterogeneity the Method section distinguishes.

Splitting the variance of each quantity on the held-out students of fold 1 into a between-school part (the variance of school means) and a within-school part, 30-56% of the variance of each weight lies between schools and the remainder within at ICC 0.30 and σ = 100.
The between-school part reflects the school-level covariates and the school random effects that the candidates represent differently, and the within-school part reflects student characteristics.

The weight on M6, the IMMIG random-slope model, is the clearest case: it correlates 0.92 to 1.00 with the student's immigration indicator in every condition, so students with and without an immigrant background in the same school are predicted by different mixtures of specifications.
The identified intercept behaves differently.
Its between-school share is 20-22% at σ = 10 and 36-49% at σ = 100, and it is uncorrelated with every covariate (all correlations below 0.07 in absolute value).

The part of the outcome that the candidates miss is therefore spread over students and schools rather than concentrated in a subgroup, which is what one expects when every candidate omits four of the five random slopes that the data-generating model contains.
